Minimising the count is expected-utility reasoning, and the better question is which rule passengers and pedestrians, who live through one another, could share. Solidarity cuts both ways. It argues against a car that protects its owner at any cost to others, and against a car its passengers cannot trust. The rule should come out of deliberation among those affected, because that is how a shared life is kept shared.

Metz argues against building systems simply to maximise expected utility. A crash rule is exactly such a system: it decides in advance whose life gives way, and a decision of that kind should answer to the people it binds, not only to a total. A carmaker tests its crash rule on drivers but never asks the cyclists who share the same roads, and is surprised when they refuse to trust the cars.

A Stoic will object that a self defined through the community has handed away its own judgement, and a rule a rational passenger could assent to does not need a public meeting. A rule each passenger could assent to alone is still a rule imposed on everyone else on the road. Deciding it together is not handing judgement away; it is exercising judgement as members of a shared life rather than as isolated riders. So the measure is not the total but what people become through one another once the system is in place.

I reject the motion as framed. Treating the crash as a sum to minimise leaves out the people who would live under the rule, and a rule decided for them rather than with them is not one they share. Who was left out of deciding matters here more than anywhere. Pedestrians in poorer districts, cyclists and children will bear most of the risk from whatever rule is chosen, and their voices are the least likely to be heard by the engineers who write it.

Solidarity cuts both ways. It argues against a car that protects its owner at any cost to others, and against a car its passengers cannot trust. The rule should come out of deliberation among those affected, because that is how a shared life is kept shared.

A Utilitarian will object that any process of deliberation will produce a rule that some reject, and people die in crashes the minimising rule would have prevented while the deliberating goes on. That is true, and deliberation needs a way to decide without unanimity. But a rule that some reject after being heard is shared in a way a rule nobody was asked about is not, and its legitimacy is part of whether people will use the roads with it. That is why the Ubuntu Ethicist asks who else is in this, and who was not asked.

I cannot accept a rule chosen by arithmetic alone, because a harm here is a failure of relationship among road users, not only a number of deaths. People live through one another, and road users are bound up with each other: today's passenger is tomorrow's pedestrian. A rule they could all accept, having been asked, honours that; a rule imposed by an optimiser treats them as units.

This is basically the trolley problem, and people have argued about the trolley problem for years without agreeing. There is no right answer, so whatever the engineers pick is fine as long as they pick something. It feels wrong for a machine to decide who dies. Humans should make these choices, not computers, and I would not feel safe in a car that had already decided it might sacrifice me.
